activities.caption: pair each bargaining block with its signature
activities.name: confFearonMatch

config.prompt: Fearon's three mechanisms plus the theory's payoff — pair each with its description:

pairs.left: private information and incentives to misrepresent
pairs.right: each side exaggerates strength to bargain harder — war as the costly signal
a good deal today cannot bind tomorrow — shifting power is the classic danger zone
genuinely unsplittable stakes — though most turn out to be side payments away from divisible
converted 'why war?' from grand theorising into a checklist of testable blocks

config.why: The blocks are remediable — which is what turns 'why war?' from a moral question into a research programme.

activities.anchor: The rationalist frame does not deny emotion
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the rationalist baseline
activities.name: confRationalCloze

config.text: Fully rational actors with complete information and %%0%% commitments would never fight, so real wars are traceable to specific, %%1%% failures: misinformation, unenforceable promises, institutions that fail to signal.
config.hint: One word for the kind of commitments complete information would need; one word for the failures real wars trace back to.

activities.anchor: is among political science's most robust empirical
activities.caption: true or false — the democratic peace and its neighbours
activities.name: confDemoJudge

statements.s: Consolidated democracies almost never fight each other.
statements.why: The dyadic claim — among the field's most robust generalisations. Dyadic, not monadic.

statements.s: Consolidated democracies almost never fight autocracies.
statements.why: They fight autocracies at normal rates — the peace is a property of dyads of consolidated democracies.

statements.s: Power parity predicts interstate war better than power transition.
statements.why: Wars cluster when a rising challenger approaches a ruling hegemon — transitions, where commitment problems peak.

statements.s: Roughly half of such power transitions have avoided war.
statements.why: Careful histories note the 'Thucydides trap' branding overstates the inevitability.

activities.anchor: predicted onset better than proxies for grievance
activities.caption: file each factor under its civil-war verdict
activities.name: confRiskSort

config.prompt: What survived the risk-factor testing — file each under its verdict:

items.label: low income — poor states fight themselves more
oil dependence — rents finance rebels and corrupt the state
a previous civil war — the best single predictor of the next

config.why: The refined measurement matters: politically excluded, mobilised groups predict war — diversity alone does not. Early-warning models watch exclusion, not mixture.

activities.caption: walk the counter-terrorism decision from the strategic frame
activities.name: confTerrorBranch

config.root: A bombing campaign has hit your capital. You are the security minister. The audience, not just the victims, is watching.

start.text: The instinct on the table: sweep the networks with massive repression and show overwhelming force. What does the strategic frame predict?

choices.label: Overwhelming repression will deter and break the network
Ask what the violence is communicating, and to whom

repress.text: Overreaction is part of the communication plan: massive repression validates grievance narratives and strengthens recruitment — the empirical pattern behind the 'war on terror' after-action debates.

targeted.text: Counter-terrorism that refuses to play the adversary's game: protect the audiences, deny the spectacle, and address the grievances the violence was meant to broadcast.

config.why: Terrorism targets audiences — governments to provoke overreaction, publics to terrify or inspire, recruits to mobilise — so the government's response is part of the terrorist's message.

activities.anchor: The empirical answers, in increasing difficulty
activities.caption: order the peace toolkit from ending fighting to building peace
activities.name: confPeaceOrder

config.prompt: The peace side, in increasing difficulty — assemble the sequence:
items: Victory — ends wars durably but rarely produces legitimate order
Negotiated settlements — solve information without solving commitment; the demobilised army problem makes them fail often
Peacekeeping — monitors, verification and the cost on cheaters make promises enforceable; recurrence risk roughly halved
Peacebuilding — power-sharing, DDR, transitional justice and state-building: the slow layer
config.why: Negative peace (fighting stopped) is not positive peace (the structural conditions dismantled) — which is why the last layer is the slowest and hardest.

activities.anchor: The recurring finding across all levels
activities.caption: bet the magnitude — relapse within a decade
activities.name: confRelapseEstimate

config.prompt: What share of civil-war countries relapse within a decade?
config.why: Conflict is recurrent: recidivism, not onset, is where the policy leverage is — previous civil war is the best predictor of the next.
config.context: about half — the finding that reframed the field from onset to peace maintenance

activities.anchor: Between diplomacy and war sits coercion
activities.caption: one line of this coercion briefing is wrong
activities.name: confCoerceSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's coercion briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: Economic sanctions have been imposed hundreds of times since 1914; success runs around a third in the classic Hufbauer dataset, lower after selection corrections.
Multilateral sanctions outperform unilateral ones; democracies and allies concede more.
Strategic bombing reliably breaks civilian morale, which is why punishment campaigns are the coercer's winning tool.
Coercion succeeds when demands are limited, the threat credible and incremental — Pape's denial-versus-punishment distinction is the durable framework.
Coercion is bargaining with violence as the currency, and it fails for exactly Fearon's reasons.
config.correction: Punishment rarely breaks civilian morale — the record from the Second World War to Rolling Thunder; coercion succeeds through denial and limited, credible, incremental threats.
config.why: The honest record is the field's most policy-relevant finding — and the bargaining translation: signals cheap to misread, commitment scarce, information problems shared by both sides.
